issue_context.title: CopySign is slow
issue_context.body:
<!--This is just a template - feel free to delete any and all of it and replace as appropriate.-->

### Description

```C#
        [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)]
        public static int CopySign_A1(int value, int sign) {
            return int.CopySign(value, sign);
        }

        [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining)]
        public static int SignZeroToOne(Int32 value) {
            return (value >> (32 - 1)) - (~value >> (32 - 1));
        }

        [MethodImpl(MethodImplOptions.AggressiveInlining | MethodImplOptions.AggressiveOptimization)]
        public static int CopySign_A2(int value, int sign) {
            if (int.MinValue != value || 0 > sign) {
                return value * SignZeroToOne(value ^ sign);
            }
            return checked(-value);
        }
```
CopySign_A2 is mush faster than CopySign_A1.

### Configuration

.NET 7 RC

### Data

Random inputs (x10000)

X64 RyuJIT AVX2 (Coffee Lake)

|           Method |      Mean |     Error |    StdDev |
|----------------- |----------:|----------:|----------:|
|           Test_0 |  3.093 us | 0.0064 us | 0.0060 us |
| Test_CopySign_A1 | 25.423 us | 0.4784 us | 0.4475 us |
| Test_CopySign_A2 |  6.486 us | 0.1288 us | 0.1323 us |

Test_0: nop

this attribute is redundant (the method is getting inlined anyway)

```suggestion
```

nit: While this is below the RyuJIT always inline size, and effectively has no impact in RyuJIT, that may not be true for all possible compilers that handle this code. Mono has different limits for example, and there are scenarios where code will only be inlined when its been attributed.

`MethodImplOptions` is one of the runtime attributes that has a specialized encoding in the method declaration, so we aren't wasting any space by specifying these and it can only help ensure our intent is followed on other runtimes.

@tannergooding thanks for the explanation, I was not aware of that.

@jkotas @stephentoub in the past you have often asked me to remove similar annotations. What is our strategy for methods that get inlined by RyuJIT without the attribute being applied?

The unnecessary annotations are code clutter. It is better to omit them if one can reasonably expect the method to be naturally inlined.

This method has 6 trivial IL instructions, so it is reasonable to expect that it is going to be inlined by any optimizing code generator.

I don't think we can give that expectation to Mono at this time. There are a number of improvements still needed to their inliner before it will work as expected for an optimizing code generator. 

For example, mono only allows inlining methods that contain a constructor call if they are marked `AggressiveInlining` today and there was a discussion on that here: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/84660#discussion_r1164500106

There are many similar pessimizations and while this particular case might work, this is ultimately an internal helper method and the clutter is really not that bad. It's no worse than many of the other attributes we have in places and is easily skimmed over.

It also allows us to trivially identify methods we expect to be always inlined and can even improve things in RyuJIT in some cases since our "always inline" threshold isn't actually "always inline". It can still be skipped due to general budget limitations (for which `AggressiveInlining` can minimally increase) and can depend on the exact `InlinePolicy` being used. 

-- We are notably inconsistent in what this "always inline" threshold is and whether it is actually respected. For example the `DefaultPolicy` only skips for `12 bytes`, while `ALWAYS_INLINE_SIZE` is defined as `16`. We similarly make an observation of `CALLEE_BELOW_ALWAYS_INLINE_SIZE`, but never actually use that outside the CSV dump. We allow the `RandomPolicy` to ignore this as well (also soft coding it as `16`, rather than using the constant), we only use `m_CodeSize` as part of the general estimate for `ExtendedDefaultPolicy`, etc.

So I think there is likely still work needed to ensure that code size alone is functionally treated at least as equivalently as `AggressiveInlining` in RyuJIT.

> that may not be true for all possible compilers that handle this code

A notable mention would be Unity IL2CPP which by default doesn't inline across types if `AggresiveInlining` isn't specified.

For now this'd only affect OOB packages available for .Net Standard though, but when Unity updates to .Net 8 it'll also affect inbox code.

I agree that there is a grey area where the inlining thresholds differ between Mono or between different RyuJIT heuristics.

If the method is a trivial wrapper for another method, a trivial property getter or a trivial expression (e.g. no more than 3 ops), I think it is a reasonable to expect that the method will be inlined even without AggressiveInlining annotation.
I logged https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/94349 to track some of the potentially issues I noticed with the RyuJIT handling of the `always inline threshold`.

> A notable mention would be Unity IL2CPP which by default doesn't inline across types if AggresiveInlining isn't specified.

It does not make sense to tell everyone to mark all trivial methods with AggresiveInlining to make them inline with IL2CPP. It is a problem for IL2CPP to solve.

IL2CPP depends on the C/C++ compiler for inlining. I believe that inlining in IL2CPP works just fine with link time codegen that is recommended for best performance. The problem only occurs for fast-build configurations without link time codegen or when link time codegen is not available. IL2CPP duplicates AggresiveInlining methods in every complication unit as a workaround for these cases. They can duplicate other trivial methods as well (if they are not doing it already). It is a tradeoff between build time and runtime performance.

> I believe that inlining in IL2CPP works just fine with link time codegen that is recommended for best performance.

The issue would be that Unity doesn't enable LTCG/LTO in the default configuration, you can enable it in newer versions in the settings. Not sure how many people do so though.
According to the docs, LTCG should be enabled by default in the master configuration that is recommended for shipping bits: https://docs.unity3d.com/ScriptReference/Il2CppCompilerConfiguration.html

> in the master configuration that is recommended for shipping bits

That's right but the default configuration is Release, not Master.

`Int128.` is unnecessary as we are in the `Int128` type

I'm notably not really a fan of this additional complexity to maintain two copies of the code. 32-bit is already extremely pessimized for `Int128` and I don't think it's worth the additional micro-optimizations here. Just have the singular code path that is consistent with the other types instead.

I'd just do this the simple/readable way as:
```suggestion
            if ((value == Int128.MinValue) && IsPositive(sign))
```

The JIT should take care of inlining the comparison and IsPositive check to give good codegen.

The `SameSign` operation can even be optimized for `32-bit` platforms by only comparing the upper half of `_upper`, which is a much more reasonable platform specific optimization and keeps it heavily isolated away to only where needed.
